frontend.prompt:
Scope (frontend-only): implement UI and client-side data-handling so that ordinary (non-owner, non-superuser) users never see other users' resources when the backend enforces the described behavior. Do not change backend; rely only on the explicit API facts below.

Preserved API facts (explicit — must be assumed exactly as stated):
- For ordinary users, when they attempt GET, PUT or DELETE on another user's existing item, the backend will return HTTP 404 with response body detail="Item not found". 
- When the item truly does not exist, the backend will return the same HTTP 404 and same detail="Item not found" response. 
- Owner and superuser permissions are unchanged by this behavior (they retain their previous access). 
- The list endpoint continues to return only items visible to the current user (server-side filtering remains in place).

Frontend implementation requirements and concrete instructions (covering every applicable requirement and preserved constraint):
1) Global handling rule
- Treat any HTTP 404 response on item-level GET, PUT or DELETE as a canonical Not Found for the current user. The UI must not differentiate whether the 404 came from "item does not exist" or "item exists but belongs to another user". Both must produce identical visible behavior and messaging.
- Do not display or reveal any data that would indicate the resource exists for another user (no leaked details from error messages, response bodies, or caches).

2) Unified UX messaging
- For 404 responses on item-level GET/PUT/DELETE, display a neutral "Item not found" message (use the backend text exactly or your localized equivalent), and offer navigation back to the item list. Do not show "Permission denied", "Forbidden", or any owner/ownership clues.
- Implement a single NotFound UI (component/page/modal) used for these cases so the experience is consistent.

3) Detail (GET) requests
- Always perform a network GET to the item detail endpoint when navigating to a detail or edit page. Do not show cached detail data without a successful network verify first.
- If GET returns 200: render the returned item normally (owners and superusers will still see their data). If GET returns 404: discard any cached item detail, show the NotFound UI, and remove the item from local caches/stores if present.
- If GET returns other errors (500/timeout): show a neutral error message for server errors; do not conflate these with 404 handling.

4) Update (PUT/PATCH) requests
- For update flows that use optimistic UI, disable or guard optimistic commits when the update target is user-owned critical info; otherwise ensure immediate revert logic is in place if the request returns 404.
- When a PUT/PATCH returns 200/204: accept the response per normal.
- When a PUT/PATCH returns 404: treat as Not Found — revert any optimistic changes, remove the item from local store, display the NotFound UI or notification "Item not found", and redirect user to their item list if they are on an edit page.
- Do not display permission hints or details about the owning user.

5) Delete (DELETE) requests
- When DELETE returns 200/204: remove item from UI/store and show success per normal.
- When DELETE returns 404: treat as Not Found — remove the item from UI/store if still present (it is not visible to the current user), show the NotFound UI or a neutral notification "Item not found", and do not surface authorization details. Do not show an error that indicates the server is hiding existence for ownership reasons.

6) Lists and client-side caching
- Always source the master list from the server list endpoint (the backend guarantees it includes only the current user's visible items). Do not reconstitute or display items that are not returned by that list endpoint.
- If you persist an item list in local cache (store, localStorage, IndexedDB), reconcile with the server list on navigation or periodic sync: any cached item not present in the server-provided list should be removed from displayed lists and caches (do not present it to the user).
- If a cached list contains an item and a subsequent detail GET returns 404 for that item, remove it from the cache and UI immediately and show NotFound behavior if user was viewing it.

7) Authorization & UI affordances
- Continue to show edit/delete UI controls to users only according to the existing client-side authorization rules you already use for owners/superusers. Do not change those controls because of the new 404 behavior; however, be prepared to handle 404 responses when a non-owner attempts an action (the server will return 404).
- If the client uses any pre-checks (role checks, ownership flags), keep them; but always gracefully handle server-side 404s for the three operations.

8) Error handling and logging
- Log 404 occurrences in client-side diagnostics (for developers) with full request context, but never surface logs to users that could indicate another user's existence.
- For user-facing messages, always use the neutral NotFound UI/message described above for 404s; for other status codes use their appropriate messages.

9) Navigation behavior
- If a user is viewing an item detail or edit page and receives a 404 from GET/PUT/DELETE, immediately redirect them to the item list (or display the NotFound UI with a clear button to return to the list). Do not remain on the detail/edit screen displaying stale data.

10) Tests to add (frontend):
- Unit/integration tests that assert: GET detail 404 triggers NotFound UI and clears cache; PUT 404 reverts optimistic update (or cancels update) and clears cache; DELETE 404 removes item from list and shows NotFound message.
- E2E tests that simulate: list contains only user's items; navigating to an item for which GET returns 404 shows NotFound and does not leak data.

11) Implementation checklist (developer tasks)
- Implement a central HTTP response handler that interprets 404 for item-level endpoints as NotFound (apply to GET/PUT/DELETE). Keep other handlers unchanged.
- Reuse single NotFound UI component for all these 404 cases.
- Ensure client caches/stores (Redux, Vuex, MobX, localStorage) remove items when 404 received for that item.
- Ensure optimistic updates are reverted on 404 for PUT/PATCH.
- Ensure DELETE 404 causes removal from UI/store and NotFound UX.
- Add unit/integration/E2E tests for the three operations.

12) Minimal code patterns / pseudocode (translate to your stack):
- fetchDetail(id):
    response = await GET /items/{id}
    if response.status == 200: render response.body
    else if response.status == 404: clearCache(item id); showNotFound(); redirectToList();
    else: showServerError();

- updateItem(id, payload):
    // if optimistic: save previous state
    response = await PUT /items/{id} payload
    if response.status in (200,204): applyResponse();
    else if response.status == 404: revertOptimistic(); clearCache(id); showNotFound(); redirectToList();
    else: showServerError();

- deleteItem(id):
    response = await DELETE /items/{id}
    if response.status in (200,204): removeFromStore(id); showSuccess();
    else if response.status == 404: removeFromStore(id); showNotFound();
    else: showServerError();

Notes and constraints to follow strictly
- Do not attempt to interpret 404 as a permission error in the UI for these cases. The explicit requirement is that ordinary users see 404/not-found and must not be shown resource existence or ownership clues.
- Preserve owner and superuser behavior: nothing in front-end should block owners or superusers from their existing access flows; that will be enforced by the server and the above handling will still allow 200 responses for owners/superusers.
- Do not assume any other server behaviors beyond the explicit facts above.

Deliverable: implement the above changes in your frontend codebase: centralize 404 handling for item-level GET/PUT/DELETE, remove stale/cached items on 404, display a unified NotFound UI, and add tests to verify behavior. Ensure no UI flows reveal information about resources owned by other users.

backend.prompt:
Scope: implement backend-only changes so that, for ordinary authenticated users, any attempt to GET, PUT, or DELETE an item that belongs to another user returns HTTP 404 with body {"detail": "Item not found"}. Nonexistent items must produce the exact same HTTP 404 + {"detail": "Item not found"}. Do not change owner or superuser privileges (they keep their current access). Do not change list endpoints' behavior: lists must continue to return only items visible to the current user. Do not change frontend behavior.

Implementation instructions (backend engineers):

1) Principle and invariants (must be preserved and applied everywhere)
   - Invariant A: Owners and superusers retain their current permissions and behavior; do not alter their authorization checks.
   - Invariant B: Listing endpoints remain unchanged and must continue to return only data visible to the requesting user.
   - Invariant C: For an authenticated ordinary user (not owner, not superuser) requesting another user's item via GET, PUT, DELETE, the response must be HTTP 404 with body exactly {"detail": "Item not found"}.
   - Invariant D: If the requested item does not exist, the response must be identical to Invariant C (HTTP 404, same JSON body).
   - Invariant E: If the request is unauthenticated, preserve the existing authentication behavior (e.g., 401) — do not change global auth semantics unless explicitly required by policy.
   - Invariant F: No client-visible metadata (status codes, headers, body content) may leak whether an item existed but the user lacked permission; the observable response for "not found" vs "forbidden" must be the same for ordinary authenticated users.

2) API endpoints in scope
   - Single-item endpoints that accept an item identifier and support GET, PUT, DELETE (e.g., /items/{id}).
   - Also apply same behavior to HEAD if implemented for the resource.

3) Authorization flow (replace current per-item unauthorized responses with not-found for ordinary users)
   - Step 1: Authenticate the request as usual. If unauthenticated, return the existing auth response (typically 401). Do not convert unauthenticated responses to 404.
   - Step 2: Load the item by ID from the primary datastore using the same query used previously. If item lookup returns no row, immediately return:
       HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
       Content-Type: application/json
       Body: {"detail": "Item not found"}
   - Step 3: If item exists, evaluate whether the requesting user is the owner of the item OR the requesting user is a superuser/has the pre-existing elevated permission that still must be honored. If owner or superuser: allow the normal behavior for GET/PUT/DELETE (no change).
   - Step 4: If item exists and user is authenticated but is not owner and is not superuser, do NOT return 403 or any other status. Instead, return the same 404 response used in Step 2:
       HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
       Content-Type: application/json
       Body: {"detail": "Item not found"}
     Also: do not perform any side effects, audits notwithstanding, and do not expose item contents, headers that reveal state (see section 5).

4) PUT / DELETE specifics
   - For PUT and DELETE, perform the same checks in the same order and with the same responses:
     * Authenticate -> if unauthenticated, behave as before.
     * Attempt to load item -> if not found, respond 404 + {"detail": "Item not found"}.
     * If found and user is owner or superuser -> perform update/delete as before.
     * If found and user is not owner nor superuser -> return 404 + {"detail": "Item not found"}, and do not perform the update/delete or partial updates, do not reveal validation errors or existence via error codes.
   - Ensure atomicity: do not modify the DB before validating owner/superuser; if the platform previously used optimistic concurrency, preserve it for owner/superuser flows.

5) Headers and metadata hygiene (prevent side-channel leaks)
   - When returning the 404 for unauthorized-or-missing, do not include headers that would reveal resource existence or allowed methods. Specifically, avoid returning Allow, ETag, Last-Modified, Link headers, or Location headers that could vary between "exists" and "does not exist" cases. If these headers are normally present for owner/superuser responses, ensure they are omitted for the 404 response.
   - If your platform automatically adds debug, trace, or detailed error payloads in non-production modes, ensure that those are not emitted to the client for these 404 responses (internal logs are acceptable but must not be sent to the client).

6) Logging and auditing
   - Log unauthorized access attempts internally (unauthorized access to existing items) for audit and security, but ensure logs are not returned to clients. Logs may include requestor id, target id, timestamp, and reason (e.g., "access denied, returned 404").
   - Ensure that log messages do not get serialized into client responses.

7) Tests to add / validation matrix (mandatory)
   - Test A (owner GET): authenticated owner requests own item -> returns current successful response (200 + body) unchanged.
   - Test B (owner PUT/DELETE): owner can modify/delete own item -> behavior unchanged.
   - Test C (superuser GET/PUT/DELETE): superuser can access other users' items -> behavior unchanged.
   - Test D (ordinary user GET existing-other): authenticated ordinary user requests an existing item owned by another user -> returns 404 + {"detail": "Item not found"}.
   - Test E (ordinary user PUT/DELETE existing-other): ordinary user tries to modify/delete another user's existing item -> returns 404 + {"detail": "Item not found"} and no changes are applied.
   - Test F (ordinary user GET/PUT/DELETE missing-id): ordinary user requests an ID that does not exist -> returns 404 + {"detail": "Item not found"} identical to Test D.
   - Test G (lists): list endpoint returns only items visible to the user (same as now) — no change.
   - Test H (unauthenticated): unauthenticated requests keep existing behavior (typically 401) — do not convert to 404.
   - Test I (headers): verify that 404 responses for unauthorized-or-missing do not include existence-revealing headers (ETag, Allow, Last-Modified, Link, Location).
   - Implement automated unit and integration tests for each HTTP method and each scenario above.

8) Implementation patterns and examples (framework-agnostic pseudocode)
   - Pseudocode for a single-item handler (applies to GET, PUT, DELETE):
       authenticate request
       if not authenticated:
           return existing_auth_response()  # do not change
       item = load_item_by_id(id)
       if item is None:
           return 404_json('Item not found')
       if current_user.is_owner(item) or current_user.is_superuser():
           proceed_with_normal_handler(item)
       else:
           return 404_json('Item not found')
   - Ensure proceed_with_normal_handler performs the exact same behavior as before for owners/superusers.

9) Deployment/rollout notes
   - This change is security-sensitive. Roll out with tests enabled and a short monitoring window to detect regressions.
   - Verify that rate-limiting, caching, and CDN layers do not cache 404 responses in a way that breaks owner/superuser access. If caching is used, set appropriate cache-control for 404 responses (no-store or short TTL) to avoid incorrect caching of access-denied-as-404.

10) Documentation and API contract
   - Update internal API docs to state: "For authenticated ordinary users, requests to item endpoints where the item either doesn't exist or exists but belongs to another user will return HTTP 404 with JSON body {\"detail\": \"Item not found\"}. Owners and superusers retain prior permissions. List endpoints unchanged."
   - Do not modify external public API docs visible to clients unless required; if you do, be explicit about the 404 semantics.

11) Do not change (explicitly preserved)
   - Do not alter owner and superuser permission checks or grant/deny logic for them.
   - Do not change list-return logic: lists must continue to restrict to visible items for the current user.
   - Do not alter unauthenticated authentication behavior (401, etc.) except for bug fixes outside the scope of these instructions.

12) Acceptance criteria (must be satisfied before merging)
   - All tests from section 7 pass.
   - Verified via integration test that ordinary user receives HTTP 404 + exact JSON body {"detail": "Item not found"} both when the item does not exist and when it exists but is owned by another user.
   - Owners and superusers can access other users' items as before.
   - List endpoints unchanged.
   - No client-visible headers or payloads leak existence or ownership information for the 404 cases.

Return exactly these changes as backend implementation work. Do not modify frontend code or assumptions; frontend will treat the 404 as specified.
